newsitem.title: USA: Stocks choppy, lower after Intel-led sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Stocks choppy, lower after Intel-led sell-off.

text.p: Stocks slipped Friday in choppy trading after Intel Corp. stunned Wall Street by warning of weaker-than-expected second-quarter profits.
At 1 p.m. EDT, the Dow Jones industrial average was down about 15.45 points, or 0.21 percent, at 7,314.73 after dropping earlier to a low of 7,242, down 80 points.
Declines beat advances by a 12-10 margin on volume of more than 295 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The technology-heavy Nasdaq composite index was also soft, down 12.47 at 1,390.57, but well up from the 47-point fall it suffered at the opening.
The 30-year Treasury bond was up 25/32, or $7.81 on a $1,000 bond. Its yield fell to 6.92 percent, down from 6.98 percent Thursday.

Intel, the world's largest computer chip maker, said it expected second-quarter revenues to drop 5 percent to 10 percent from last quarter's $6.4 billion. It said profits would fall short of industry analysts' forecasts.
The news shocked Wall Street, especially because Intel has consistently managed to beat forecasts in the past.
"Growth or momentum investors are programmed to sell at the first hint of disappointment -- and they did. Intel is a bellwether stock in one of the fastest-growing industries," one analyst said.
At 1 p.m., Intel was off 11-33/64 at 152-1.4, with more than 41 million shares traded. It tumbled as low as 137-7/8 earlier.

With only about half the trading session over, Intel was in 12th place for the highest volume in an individial issue in one session. That record is held by Comparator Systems Corp., which traded 177.7 million shares on May 7, 1996, according to the Nasdaq.
One trader said stocks recovered as investors took a closer look at Intel's forecast of gross margins of 60 percent instead of 64 percent, which does not represent a drastic falloff.
"That's just a tempest in a teapot," he said.
Once investors got over their initial scare, bargain-hunters moved in, analysts said.

Some Wall Street analysts also took comfort in the fact that Intel's warning provided evidence of a gradual slowing in the economy, which could suggest there would be no need for further interest rate increases by the Federal Reserve.

"This backs up (Fed Chairman) Alan Greenspan's decision not to raise rates. The economy is slowing, and there have to be some disappointments in the business cycle," said Chris Dickerson, an analyst at Global Market Strategists Inc.

The brightened outlook for interest rates, and the bond's move back below the psychologically important 7 percent level, sent bank stocks surging. A key banking index rose 9 points to 601, up 1.5 percent.
Chase Manhattan Corp. rose 1-5/8 to 94-1/2. Citicorp gained 3-3/4 to 113-3/8 and J.P. Morgan & Co. was up 1-7/8 at 106-1/4.

Compaq Computer Corp. defied the general malaise with a rise of 3 to 104-7/8. Its chief executive said Compaq expected to meet second-quarter earnings estimates and said the world's largest personal computer maker was having none of Intel's difficulties in Europe.
Sunglass Hut International Inc. shares were 7/8 lower at 6-3/4 after its president resigned and the retailer said its sales remained sluggish in May.
